title: Weighed in the balances (Daniel 5)
hookLine: the writing on the wall: weighed, and found wanting

lines: HOLY CUPS AT A ROYAL PARTY.
A HAND WRITES ON THE WALL.
cards: King Belshazzar has been tasting wine at his great feast when he calls for the cups: the gold and silver vessels taken out of the Temple in Jerusalem.
He and his lords, his wives and concubines drink from them, and praise gods of gold and silver, brass, iron, wood and stone.
In the same hour, the fingers of a man's hand appear and write on the plaster of the palace wall, near the lampstand. The king watches the hand write. His face changes.
In the King James words, "his knees smote one against another." Nobody in the room can read it.

teach.h: LET THY GIFTS BE TO THYSELF.
teach.b: The king's wise men fail. The queen remembers a man from the old king's days, Daniel, and he's brought in. Belshazzar offers him scarlet clothes, a gold chain, a high place in the kingdom.

Daniel's first words: "Let thy gifts be to thyself." He'll read it, but not for pay. Then, before reading, he tells the king a story the king already knows: how his father Nebuchadnezzar grew proud and was brought low.
And then: "thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this." Though you knew. The charge isn't ignorance.
It's knowing better and lifting the holy cups anyway. Then Daniel reads the wall. "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN."
Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and finished it.

teach.h: THOU ART WEIGHED IN THE BALANCES.
teach.b: Then: "TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting." Peres: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. Weighed.
Not shouted at, not argued with: put on a scale, and the scale reads light. The text doesn't linger. "In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain."
It's a frightening chapter, and it leaves a plain question for an ordinary evening: if today were set on a scale, what would be in the pans?

how: Some Jews keep a practice called cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul, looking honestly at their day or their year, especially in the month of Elul before Rosh Hashanah, and some do it each night before sleep.

o: divided, and given to the Medes and Persians
numbered, with the kingdom's days finished
weighed, and found wanting on the scale

games.q: the writing on the wall — tap the pairs.
p: divided, given to the Medes and Persians
taken from the Temple in Jerusalem

s: the king's wise men read the writing easily
none of them could read it. the queen remembered Daniel.
Daniel says the king knew better
"thou... hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this."
in Daniel's reading, tekel means divided
tekel is weighed. peres is divided.

games.q: you're Daniel. the frightened king offers you scarlet, a gold chain and a high place in the kingdom if you read the wall. what do you do?
o: accept the gifts, then read it.
turn down the gifts, then read it plainly.
refuse to read it at all.
games.why: "Let thy gifts be to thyself." he reads the wall for nothing, and doesn't soften a word of it.

practice: Picture an old balance scale and go back over today so far, or yesterday if it's early: in one pan, what you did well, a kindness, a job done right; in the other, what was wanting, a sharp word, a time you knew better.

Don't argue with the scale or punish yourself with it; just look, and choose one good thing to add to the first pan before tonight. If you pray, bring both pans before God in words from your tradition.

wordCard.voice: Tekel. The word on the wall that Daniel reads as weighed, and found wanting. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: the third word on the wall, which Daniel reads as weighed (Daniel 5:25–27).

carryVoice: Your line: weighed in the balance. The charge wasn't ignorance; it was knowing better. Day eight hundred seventy-one, done.
